promptDecks.title: Understanding Emotions
promptDecks.description: Helps clients recognize, understand, and make sense of their emotions, including what triggers them, how they feel in the body, and what they may be communicating.

prompts.text: What are emotions, and why do people have them?
Why do you think humans have feelings?
What do you think emotions are trying to tell us?
Are all emotions useful in some way?
Can an emotion feel bad but still have an important purpose?
Can you have an emotion without knowing why you feel it?
Do feelings always match what is happening around you?
Can two people experience the same situation and feel differently?
Why do you think people react differently to the same events?
Are emotions something we choose, or something that happens to us?
What is the difference between having a feeling and acting on a feeling?
Can a feeling be real even if the thought behind it is not accurate?
Can you dislike a feeling without needing it to disappear?
How do you know what emotion you are feeling?
What clues help you identify your emotions?
What does a strong emotion feel like in your body?
Where do you notice emotions in your body first?
How does your body tell you something is changing emotionally?
What happens to your face when you feel different emotions?
How does your voice change when your emotions change?
How does your energy change with different emotions?
How do you know when your mood has shifted?
What emotions are easiest for you to recognize?
What emotions are harder for you to name?
What feelings do you notice in yourself most often?
What feelings do you usually hide from other people?
What emotion do people notice first about you?
What emotion do people sometimes miss?
What does happiness feel like for you?
What does sadness feel like for you?
What does anger feel like for you?
What does fear feel like for you?
What does excitement feel like for you?
What does embarrassment feel like for you?
What does disappointment feel like for you?
What does pride feel like for you?
What does calm feel like for you?
What does frustration feel like for you?
What emotion is easiest for you to talk about?
What emotion is hardest for you to talk about?
What emotion do you think people misunderstand most?
What emotion do you wish other people understood better?
Can you feel two opposite emotions at the same time?
When have you felt happy and sad at the same time?
When have you felt excited and nervous at the same time?
When have you felt angry and hurt at the same time?
When have you felt proud and uncomfortable at the same time?
Why do you think emotions can be complicated?
How can two different feelings both make sense?
What happens when you only pay attention to one emotion and ignore another?
What emotions often show up together for you?
What feelings are easier to notice after another feeling goes away?
How do your thoughts change when your emotions change?
How can the same situation look different depending on how you feel?
How can emotions influence what you pay attention to?
How can strong emotions affect problem solving?
How can you tell the difference between a feeling and a fact?
What is something your emotions have convinced you of before?
Have you ever felt something strongly and later saw the situation differently?
How can you respect your feelings while still checking your thoughts?
What do your emotions make you want to do?
Do feelings always tell you what action to take?
What happens when you act immediately on a strong emotion?
What happens when you ignore your emotions completely?
How can you listen to your emotions without letting them control everything?
What helps you pause before reacting?
What choices become harder when emotions are intense?
What choices become easier when you understand your emotions?
What happens when you try to push away a feeling?
Why do you think people sometimes avoid certain emotions?
What feelings are uncomfortable for you to sit with?
Can an uncomfortable emotion still be safe?
What would it look like to allow a feeling without fighting it?
What would you say to a friend who was feeling something difficult?
How could you offer yourself that same kindness?
What does it mean to accept a feeling without liking it?
Can a feeling pass without you needing to solve it?
What emotions have you learned more about as you have grown?
What have your emotions taught you about yourself?
What feelings help you understand what matters to you?
What emotions help you notice when something is important?
What emotions help you connect with other people?
What emotions help you protect yourself?
What emotions help you grow?
If your emotions were colors, what colors would they be?
If your emotions were weather, what kinds of weather would they create?
If your feelings were a language, what words would they use most often?
If your emotions had a volume button, which ones would you turn up or down?
If your emotions were messengers, what messages would they bring?
If your emotions lived in a house, what rooms would they each have?
If your emotions could introduce themselves, what would they say?
If your emotions had a team meeting, what would they discuss?
If your emotions were characters in a story, who would they be?
If your Wise Mind listened to all your emotions, what would it say?
What is one thing you understand better about your emotions?
What emotion do you want to understand better?
What emotion do you want to become more comfortable feeling?
What is one thing your emotions have taught you about yourself?
What is one reminder you want when emotions feel overwhelming?
What is one sentence you want to remember about feelings?

promptDecks.title: Acceptance & Willingness
promptDecks.description: Explore how making room for difficult internal experiences can reduce struggle and help you keep moving toward what matters, without requiring you to like, approve of, or get rid of what you feel.

prompts.text: What does acceptance mean to you?
What is the difference between accepting something and liking it?
What is the difference between acceptance and giving up?
What is something difficult you are dealing with right now?
What feelings are hardest for you to allow yourself to have?
What emotions do you usually want to get rid of as quickly as possible?
What thoughts are hardest to let be there without fighting them?
What sensations in your body are hardest to tolerate?
What happens when you try really hard not to feel something?
What happens when you tell yourself you should not feel the way you feel?

promptDecks.title: Thoughts, Feelings & Behaviors
promptDecks.description: Helps clients understand how situations, thoughts, feelings, and behaviors influence one another while recognizing personal patterns and identifying places where changing one part of the cycle can shift what happens next.

prompts.text: Think of a recent moment when your mood changed quickly. What happened, and what do you think caused the shift?
Think of a recent situation that brought up a strong feeling. What was going through your mind at the time?
Think of a recent situation that went better than you expected. What were you telling yourself while it was happening?

Think of a time you wanted to give up but kept going. What helped change what you did next?
Think of a time your feelings pushed you toward a choice you later regretted. What might have helped interrupt that pattern?
Think of a time you had a strong feeling but chose not to act on your first urge. What helped you make a different choice?
Think of a recent difficult moment. What did you do that helped the feeling pass or become more manageable?
Think of a recent difficult moment. Did anything you did accidentally keep the feeling going longer?
Think of something you do when you're anxious. How does it help in the moment, and what happens afterward?
Think of something you do when you're angry. How does that response affect what happens next?
Think of something you do when you're sad. Does it usually help your mood recover, keep it the same, or make it harder?
Think of something you do when you're overwhelmed. What effect does it have on your thoughts and feelings afterward?
Think of something you do that reliably improves your mood, even a little. What do you notice afterward?
Think of a recent day when your mood was low. What did you do that day, and how might your actions have affected your mood?
Think of a recent day when you felt pretty good. What were you doing differently?
Think of a time you changed what you were doing and your feelings eventually changed too. What did you learn from that?
Think of a time you couldn't change how you felt right away but still made a helpful choice. What happened next?
Think of a situation where your thoughts and your actions seemed to feed each other. What kept the cycle going?
Think of a pattern you get stuck in sometimes. What usually happens first, and what tends to happen next?
Think of a pattern you'd like to change. Where in the cycle of thoughts, feelings, and actions would it be easiest to interrupt it?
Think of a recent situation you wish had gone differently. If you could change just one thought or action from that moment, what would you change?
Think of something difficult that may happen soon. What thoughts, feelings, and urges do you expect might show up?
Think of something difficult that may happen soon. What could you do even if the uncomfortable thoughts or feelings still show up?

Think of a situation where two different thoughts could lead to two very different reactions. What are the two thoughts?

A friend seems unusually quiet around you. What might your brain assume before you actually know what's happening?
Someone laughs while you're talking. What are several possible explanations for the laughter?

Can a thought feel completely true and still turn out to be wrong? What is an example?
Can a feeling give you important information without proving that your thoughts about the situation are true? What might that look like?
Can you still make a helpful choice when your thoughts haven't changed yet? What might that look like?
Can changing what you do eventually change what you think or feel? What is an example?
Can changing the way you think about something change what you do next? What is an example?
What kinds of thoughts tend to make problems feel bigger for you?
What kinds of thoughts help you slow down before reacting?
What kinds of thoughts make you want to avoid something?
What kinds of thoughts make you more willing to try?
What kinds of situations make it hardest for you to notice what you're thinking before you react?
Which do you usually notice first when something is wrong: your thoughts, your feelings, your body, or what you want to do?
Which is hardest for you to notice in the moment: your thoughts, your feelings, your body, or your actions?
When your emotions become intense, what tends to happen to the way you think?
When your emotions become intense, what tends to happen to the choices you make?
When you're feeling calm, what becomes easier to see about a difficult situation?
What is one thought, feeling, and behavior pattern you've gotten better at recognizing?
What is one pattern you keep finding yourself in even though you know it isn't helping?
What usually keeps that pattern going?
What tends to help break that pattern?
What is one reaction that gives you relief right away but sometimes creates a bigger problem later?
What is one choice that can feel harder in the moment but usually helps you later?
What is one small action that can change the direction of a difficult day?
What is something you can do when you can't control the situation but you can control how you respond?
What is one thought you would like to get better at noticing before you automatically believe it?
What is one behavior you would like to experiment with changing just to see what happens?
What is one connection between your thoughts, feelings, and actions that you've noticed about yourself?
What is one part of your own thoughts-feelings-behaviors cycle you'd like to understand better?

promptDecks.title: Family Activities
promptDecks.description: Provides fun, playful activities families can do together during sessions to build connection, cooperation, communication, and positive shared experiences through games, creativity, movement, and silliness.

promptDecks.title: Conflict Resolution
promptDecks.description: Helps clients practice navigating disagreements, understanding different perspectives, communicating needs, and working toward solutions while managing emotions and maintaining healthy boundaries.

prompts.text: You and a friend both want to choose what game to play, and neither of you wants to give in. What could you say?
A friend keeps changing the rules of a game when they start losing. What could you say?
You are playing a game with a friend, and they accuse you of cheating even though you did not cheat. What could you say?
You think your friend cheated during a game, but they say they did not. What could you say?
You and a friend remember what happened during an argument differently. What could you say?
A friend tells you that you hurt their feelings, but you did not mean to. What could you say?
You tell a friend that they hurt your feelings, and they say, “It was just a joke.” What could you say?
You apologize to a friend, and they are still upset with you. What could you do?
A friend apologizes to you, but you are still upset and need some time. What could you say?
You accidentally break something that belongs to your sibling. What could you say?
Your sibling breaks something that belongs to you and says it was an accident. What could you say?
You and your sibling both say you were using the tablet first. How could you solve the problem?
You and your sibling are arguing about whose turn it is to sit in the front seat. How could you solve the problem?
Your sibling keeps coming into your room after you have asked them to knock. What could you say?
Your sibling is using something of yours without asking. What could you say?
You borrowed something from your sibling and forgot to return it. Now they are angry. What could you say?
You and your sibling are both blaming each other for a mess. What could you do?
Your parent tells you to turn off a game right when you are in the middle of something important. What could you say?
Your parent says you cannot do something you were really looking forward to. What could you say?
You think a rule at home is unfair. How could you talk to your parent about it?

You said something mean to a family member because you were angry. What could you do afterward?
You slam a door during an argument and later wish you had handled it differently. What could you do?
You and a friend planned to hang out, but they change the plan without asking you. What could you say?
Your friend wants to do one thing and you want to do something completely different. How could you find a solution?
Your friend always wants to decide what you do together. What could you say?
You choose the activity this time, but your friend looks disappointed. What could you do?
A friend says they are tired of always doing what you want. What could you say?

You join a game and another kid gets angry because they think you changed the rules. What could you say?
You accidentally bump into someone, and they think you did it on purpose. What could you say?

You think someone skipped your turn during a game. What could you say?

You and another person both start talking at the same time. What could you do?

promptDecks.title: Impulsivity & Emotional Regulation
promptDecks.description: Helps clients recognize patterns involving impulsive reactions and intense emotions while building greater awareness of triggers, pauses, regulation strategies, and choices that support more intentional responses.

promptDecks.title: Behavior Detective
promptDecks.description: Helps caregivers look beyond a child’s behavior to explore possible triggers, needs, skills, emotions, and environmental factors that may be contributing to what they see.

prompts.text: Think of one behavior from your child that you would like to understand better. What does the behavior look like?
Think of one behavior that has been difficult lately. When is it most likely to happen?
Think of one behavior that has been difficult lately. When is it least likely to happen?

Think of a recent difficult behavior. What did the behavior help your child get away from or delay?
Think of a behavior you find frustrating. What makes sense about that behavior when you look at the situation from your child's perspective?
Think of a behavior that seems out of proportion to the situation. What might have made the situation feel bigger to your child than it looked from the outside?
Think of a behavior that seems to happen “out of nowhere.” What early signs might be easy to miss?
Think of a behavior you want your child to stop doing. What would you like your child to be able to do instead?
Think of something your child struggles to do consistently. What skill might still be developing?

Think of a task your child regularly avoids. What might make starting or completing that task difficult?
Think of a transition your child struggles with. What part of the transition seems hardest?
Think of a limit your child has difficulty accepting. What might be especially hard about that limit?
Think of a situation where your child becomes overwhelmed quickly. What demands are being placed on them all at once?
Think of a difficult interaction with your child. What were you feeling and needing during that interaction?
Think of a difficult interaction with your child. How might your own stress have affected what happened?
Think of a difficult interaction with your child. How did your response affect what happened next?
Think of a recent difficult moment with your child. What seemed to help the situation?
Think of a recent difficult moment with your child. What seemed to make the situation harder?
Think of a recent difficult moment that went better than usual. What was different?
Think of a time your child handled a normally difficult situation successfully. What helped make success possible?
Think of a situation where your child does well with one adult but struggles with another. What might be different about the support, expectations, or environment?
Think of a behavior that has improved over time. What may have helped it improve?
Think of something your child is learning to handle better. What strengths are helping them?
Think of a situation where your child thrives. What conditions seem to bring out their best?

Think of a behavior you want to understand. What are three possible explanations besides “my child is choosing to be difficult”?

Think of a difficult behavior from your child. What is one thing the behavior has helped you understand about them?

promptDecks.title: Coaching & Problem Solving
promptDecks.description: Helps caregivers work through parenting challenges by identifying what is happening, considering the child’s needs and perspective, and developing realistic strategies for responding effectively.

Think of one recurring challenge with your child. What have you already tried?

promptDecks.title: Action & Mood
promptDecks.description: escription:** Helps clients explore how activity, avoidance, routines, connection, and daily choices influence mood and energy, identify behaviors that keep low mood going, and use small purposeful actions to create opportunities for motivation, pleasure, accomplishment, and connection.

prompts.text: Think of a recent day when your mood was better than usual. What were you doing differently?

promptDecks.title: Make-Believe Problems
promptDecks.description: A deck of pretend problems where you figure out what’s happening and imagine different ways to solve it.

promptDecks.title: Reviewing the Evidence
promptDecks.description: Helps clients examine the evidence supporting and challenging a thought, distinguish facts from assumptions and feelings, and develop conclusions that reflect the full picture rather than only the information their mind notices first.

prompts.text: Think of a thought that's bothering you right now. What evidence supports it?

prompts.text: ## Mindfulness

**Description:** Helps clients practice noticing thoughts, emotions, sensations, and experiences in the present moment with awareness and less judgment, while strengthening the ability to observe, describe, participate, and return attention to what is happening now.
What do you notice around you right now?
What sounds can you notice right now?
What physical sensations can you notice right now?

What does acceptance of the present moment mean to you?

What becomes harder when you spend all your energy arguing with what is already happening?

promptDecks.description: Explore challenging choices involving fairness, honesty, loyalty, responsibility, and competing values when there may not be one clear right answer.

promptDecks.title: Is it Weird?
promptDecks.description: A deck of random habits, preferences, and behaviors where you decide: is it weird or totally normal?

prompts.text: Someone talks to themselves when they’re alone.
Someone gives names and personalities to their plants.
Someone apologizes when they bump into furniture.
Someone says “please” and “thank you” to Siri or Alexa.
Someone thinks certain numbers have personalities.
Someone thinks certain letters have personalities.
Someone thinks every school subject has a specific color.
Someone thinks certain days of the week have different personalities.
Someone has a favorite burner on the stove.
Someone has a favorite spoon and gets annoyed when it’s dirty.
Someone insists water tastes better from one specific cup.
Someone has an unofficial assigned seat everywhere they regularly go.
Someone gets annoyed when somebody sits in their usual seat even though seats aren’t assigned.
Someone reads cereal boxes while eating breakfast, even if they’ve read the same box 50 times.
Someone smells a new book before reading it.
Someone smells almost every food before taking the first bite.
Someone saves the best bite of every meal for last.
Someone eats the worst part of every meal first to get it over with.
Someone refuses to let different foods touch on the plate.
Someone mixes all the food on their plate together before eating.
Someone drinks pickle juice straight from the jar.
Someone prefers soda after it has gone flat.
Someone eats frozen waffles without heating them.
Someone puts ice cubes in milk.
Someone eats chips with chopsticks so their fingers don’t get messy.
Someone has eaten the exact same breakfast almost every day for years.
Someone will only drink certain brands of bottled water because the others taste wrong.
Someone thinks food tastes better with tiny utensils.
Someone eats dessert before dinner whenever nobody stops them.
Someone saves their favorite snacks so long that they sometimes expire.
Someone owns snacks they refuse to eat because they’re “too good to waste.”
Someone keeps tiny hotel shampoos for years but never uses them.
Someone has a collection of random rocks that are important for reasons they cannot explain.
Someone keeps movie tickets, receipts, wrappers, and other tiny objects because throwing them away feels wrong.
Someone has a drawer full of things that don't belong anywhere else.
Someone has a chair in their bedroom that hasn't been used as a chair in years because it holds clothes.
Someone knows exactly where everything is in a room that looks completely chaotic.
Someone gets annoyed when somebody else organizes their mess.
Someone actually feels more comfortable when a room is a little messy.
Someone organizes their bookshelf by color even though it makes books harder to find.
Someone changes into pajamas immediately after getting home, even if it’s the middle of the afternoon.
Someone wears the same favorite hoodie so often that other people notice.
Someone intentionally wears mismatched socks every day.
Someone has “good socks” and “bad socks.”
Someone sleeps with socks on every night.
Someone cannot understand how anyone sleeps with socks on.
Someone sleeps with one foot outside the blanket no matter how cold it is.
Someone sleeps with six or more pillows.
Someone sleeps with no pillow at all.
Someone still sleeps with the same stuffed animal they had as a little kid.
Someone needs a fan blowing to sleep even in the middle of winter.
Someone sleeps with a fan on while also using several blankets.
Someone needs the TV playing to fall asleep.
Someone cannot fall asleep if there is even a tiny sound in the room.
Someone cannot sleep if the closet door is open.
Someone takes naps on the floor on purpose.
Someone takes naps that regularly last three or four hours.
Someone voluntarily wakes up early on weekends even when they have nowhere to be.
Someone sets ten alarms instead of one.
Someone has alarms labeled things like “GET UP FOR REAL THIS TIME.”
Someone wakes up two minutes before their alarm and waits for it to ring anyway.
Someone calculates exactly how much sleep they’ll get before going to bed.
Someone invents entire fictional stories in their head before falling asleep.
Someone rehearses imaginary arguments that will probably never happen.
Someone practices a phone call out loud before making it.
Someone writes a text in Notes first because sending it directly feels too risky.
Someone sends an important text and immediately throws their phone somewhere so they don’t have to see the response.
Someone waits before opening a message because they’re nervous about what it says.
Someone has more than 10,000 unread emails and feels completely fine about it.
Someone cannot tolerate having a single unread notification.
Someone regularly has more than 50 browser tabs open.
Someone closes every browser tab the second they’re finished with it.
Someone has tens of thousands of photos on their phone.
Someone takes screenshots constantly and almost never looks at them again.
Someone scrolls through their own old social media posts for entertainment.
Someone watches their own story after posting it.
Someone has used the same profile picture for five years.
Someone changes their profile picture every few weeks.
Someone likes their own social media posts.
Someone follows people they dislike because they still want to know what they’re doing.
Someone hides in another grocery-store aisle to avoid talking to someone they know.
Someone sees someone they know in public and hopes neither of them acknowledges the other.
Someone loves making conversation with complete strangers.
Someone starts conversations with strangers in elevators.
Someone rehearses their food order before reaching the counter.
Someone looks at a restaurant’s menu online hours before going there.
Someone looks up pictures of the food before deciding what to order.
Someone reads one-star reviews of places they never plan to visit just for entertainment.
Someone reads reviews of something after they already bought it.
Someone looks up movie spoilers on purpose because not knowing what happens is stressful.
Someone refuses to watch trailers because they think trailers reveal too much.
Someone pauses movies to look up actors immediately instead of waiting until the end.
Someone watches everything with subtitles even though they can hear it perfectly.
Someone gets annoyed when other people turn subtitles on.
Someone rewatches the same show over and over instead of starting something new.
Someone skips embarrassing scenes because the secondhand embarrassment is unbearable.
Someone pauses a show during an awkward scene because they need time to recover.
Someone talks directly to characters on TV.
Someone gets genuinely angry when fictional characters make obviously bad decisions.
Someone refuses to finish the final episode of a favorite show because then it would be over.
Someone reads the last page of a book before deciding whether to read the book.
Someone dog-ears book pages even when bookmarks are available.
Someone refuses to dog-ear a book because bending a page feels like destroying it.
Someone writes all over books they own.
Someone owns dozens of books they haven't read but keeps buying more.
Someone listens to audiobooks or podcasts at 2× speed.
Someone listens to the same song over and over for hours.
Someone restarts a song before it ends because they want to hear the best part again.
Someone makes playlists for incredibly specific situations, like “walking through Target when it’s raining.”
Someone has one enormous playlist containing almost every song they like.
Someone thinks songs have colors.
Someone thinks names have colors.
Someone thinks people sometimes “look like” their names.
Someone thinks September feels more like the beginning of a new year than January.
Someone dislikes Sundays because Monday is coming.
Someone actually likes Mondays because everything feels reset.
Someone prefers rainy days to sunny days.
Someone finds thunderstorms relaxing enough to fall asleep to.
Someone wears shorts outside when everyone else is wearing coats.
Someone wears hoodies when everyone else thinks it’s way too hot.
Someone likes their bedroom freezing cold but takes extremely hot showers.
Someone showers with the bathroom lights off on purpose.
Someone sits on the shower floor just because it’s comfortable.
Someone procrastinates taking a shower and then refuses to get out once they’re in.
Someone stays wrapped in a towel for 30 minutes before getting dressed.
Someone walks around the entire house while talking on the phone.
Someone has to doodle or fidget in order to listen.
Someone looks away from people because it actually helps them listen better.
Someone closes their eyes when trying hard to remember something.
Someone sticks their tongue out when concentrating.
Someone reads random signs out loud without realizing they’re doing it.
Someone repeats a word until it stops sounding like a real word.
Someone narrates what they’re doing when nobody else is around.
Someone gives themselves pep talks out loud.
Someone says “nice” to themselves after doing something correctly.
Someone gives themselves imaginary points for completing boring tasks.
Someone races the microwave to see whether they can finish something before it beeps.
Someone treats the GPS arrival time like a personal challenge to beat.
Someone would rather injure both arms carrying groceries than make two trips.
Someone automatically counts stairs while walking up them.
Someone avoids stepping on certain cracks or tiles even though they know nothing will happen.
Someone turns boring chores into imaginary competitions.
Someone tries to finish cleaning something before the current song ends.
Someone needs a special drink or snack before doing boring errands.
Someone suddenly becomes motivated to clean their entire room when they’re supposed to be doing something else.
Someone gets their best burst of productivity around midnight.
Someone makes incredibly detailed plans and then ignores them completely.
Someone writes to-do lists and then forgets the list exists.
Someone adds something they already finished to a to-do list just so they can cross it off.
Someone needs to know the entire plan before agreeing to go somewhere.
Someone needs several days to mentally prepare for plans.
Someone agrees to plans, looks forward to them, and then wishes they were canceled when the day arrives.
Someone gets to the airport three hours early and actually enjoys waiting there.
Someone likes airports even when they aren’t traveling.
Someone enjoys wandering around stores without planning to buy anything.
Someone walks through every aisle of a store even when they only need one thing.
Someone switches checkout lines and immediately becomes convinced the old line is moving faster.
Someone silently judges people based on what is in their grocery carts.
Someone browses houses for sale online even though they have absolutely no intention of moving.
Someone looks at restaurant menus for places they will probably never visit.
Someone straightens crooked objects in places that don’t belong to them.
Someone cannot relax if a picture frame is slightly crooked.
Someone needs the TV volume to be an even number.
Someone needs the TV volume to end in 0 or 5.
Someone deliberately uses weird volume numbers because even-number rules are ridiculous.
Someone stops the microwave at one second so it never beeps.
Someone gets genuinely annoyed when another person leaves 0:01 on the microwave.
Someone cannot sleep if there is a ticking clock anywhere nearby.
Someone finds vacuum cleaners or hair dryers relaxing.
Someone loves the smell of gasoline.
Someone loves the smell of hardware stores.
Someone loves the smell of chlorine.
Someone loves the smell of coffee but hates drinking coffee.
Someone thinks food tastes better when somebody else makes it.
Someone thinks a drink tastes better when somebody else pours it.
Someone believes certain locations of the exact same fast-food chain taste better than others.
Someone judges restaurants partly by how nice their bathrooms are.
Someone refuses to eat messy food because they hate having anything on their fingers.
Someone washes their hands halfway through eating if they start feeling sticky.
Someone needs to change clothes immediately after getting home.
Someone refuses to get into bed wearing clothes they wore outside.
Someone chooses clothes almost entirely based on how the fabric feels.
Someone cuts the tags out of every shirt they buy.
Someone cannot stand the seam across the toes of their socks.
Someone refuses to buy pants that don’t have usable pockets.
Someone carries around a random rock or tiny object for no practical reason.
Someone has a lucky pen they use for important tests.
Someone has a favorite pen and can immediately tell when somebody else has used it.
Someone tests several pens before deciding which one feels right.
Someone writes reminders on their hand even though they own a phone.
Someone texts themselves things they need to remember.
Someone leaves important objects directly in front of the door so forgetting them becomes physically impossible.
Someone puts something on top of their shoes so they cannot leave without remembering it.
Someone keeps important things out where they can see them because anything put away basically stops existing.
Someone leaves browser tabs open because closing them means forgetting whatever they were supposed to do.
Someone intentionally puts an object somewhere annoying so they’ll remember to deal with it later.

promptDecks.title: Perspective Taking
promptDecks.description: Helps clients practice considering other people’s thoughts, feelings, experiences, and intentions while recognizing that different perspectives can exist without one person necessarily being wrong.

prompts.text: You wave to a friend in the hallway, but they walk past without saying anything. What are some reasons they might not have responded?
A friend gives you a very short answer when you ask them a question. What might be going on?
You text a friend and they do not answer for several hours. What are some possible reasons?
A friend usually sits with you at lunch, but today they sit somewhere else. What are some possible explanations?
You say hi to someone and they seem annoyed. What could be happening that has nothing to do with you?
Your friend cancels plans at the last minute and says they cannot come. What might be going on?
Someone laughs right after you walk into the room. What are some things they could be laughing about?
Two people whisper while you are nearby. What are some possible reasons they might be whispering?
A friend seems quieter than usual today. What are some possible reasons?
Someone does not invite you to something they are doing. What are some possible explanations?
Your friend starts spending more time with someone new. How might you see the situation, and how might your friend see it?
Your friend does not want to play the game you picked. What might they be thinking or feeling?
You want to keep playing, but your friend says they want to go home. What might be happening for each person?
You think a game is fun, but your friend thinks it is boring. How can both opinions make sense?
You love a movie that your friend hates. How could both of you have reasonable opinions about the same movie?
You think something is hilarious, but your friend does not laugh. What might explain the difference?
Your friend is excited about something you do not care about very much. How could you show interest anyway?
You are telling someone about your favorite topic, but they keep looking toward the door. What might they be trying to communicate?
You are telling a long story and the other person stops asking questions. What are some possible explanations?
Someone changes the subject while you are talking about something important to you. What might have happened?
You tell a joke and your friend suddenly gets quiet. What might they be thinking or feeling?
You tease a friend in a way that seems funny to you, but they get upset. How might the joke have felt different to them?
A friend tells you that something you said hurt their feelings, but you thought it was harmless. How could both experiences be real?
Someone says, “I’m fine,” but their voice is quiet and they are looking at the floor. What might they actually be feeling?
Someone says, “Whatever,” and walks away during a disagreement. What are some possible feelings behind their response?
Your friend says they do not care about losing a game, but they stop talking and put the game away. What might be happening?
A classmate says they are not nervous about presenting, but they keep fidgeting and checking their notes. What might they be feeling?
A kid is laughing while telling a story about something embarrassing that happened to them. Does laughing necessarily mean they were not embarrassed?
Someone smiles while receiving a compliment but quickly changes the subject. What might they be feeling?
A friend says they want to be alone after having a difficult day. What might they need from you?
A friend is crying but says they do not want to talk about what happened. What could you do that respects what they want?
A friend tells you about a problem but does not ask for advice. What might they want from you?
You try to help someone solve a problem, but they become frustrated with you. What might they have wanted instead?
Someone keeps asking whether you are okay after you already said you are fine. What might they be worried about?
You want someone to comfort you, but they immediately start giving you solutions. What might they think they are doing?
Your friend tries to cheer you up with jokes when you are upset, but the jokes make you more annoyed. What might your friend have intended?
You offer someone help and they say no. What are some reasons they might prefer to do it themselves?
A classmate refuses help with an assignment even though they are struggling. What might make accepting help difficult?
Someone does not want to answer a question in front of the class even though they know the answer. What might they be worried about?
A new student barely talks during lunch. What are some possible reasons?
A new kid stands near a game at recess but does not ask to join. What might they be hoping will happen?
Someone joins your group but barely says anything. What might help them feel more comfortable?
A classmate always wants to work alone. What are some reasons they might prefer that?
A student talks constantly during group work. What might they be trying to do?
A kid keeps making jokes when everyone is supposed to be working. What might be behind the behavior besides simply trying to cause trouble?
A classmate gets angry when the teacher corrects their work. What might the correction have felt like to them?
Someone crumples up their paper after making one mistake. What might they be thinking?
A classmate refuses to try an activity they have never done before. What might they be worried will happen?
Someone says an assignment is “stupid” before they even start it. What might be underneath that reaction?
A student keeps asking exactly what will happen during an upcoming field trip. Why might knowing the details matter to them?
A classmate becomes upset when the teacher unexpectedly changes the schedule. What might make the change difficult for them?
Your teacher tells the class to stop talking, but you were not one of the people talking. How might you see the situation, and how might the teacher see it?
A teacher reminds you about a rule you already know. What are some reasons they might remind you anyway?
You think a teacher is being unfair because they will not let you redo something. What information might the teacher be considering?
A teacher gives another student extra time on an assignment but not you. What are some things you might not know about the situation?
Another student is allowed to take breaks during class when everyone else has to keep working. Why might fair not always mean everyone gets exactly the same thing?
A student gets a consequence for something they say was an accident. How might the student and teacher see the situation differently?
Your parent reminds you three times to do something you were already planning to do. How might each of you see the situation?
Your parent says no to something that seems completely reasonable to you. What information might they be considering that you do not know?
You ask to stay up later, and your parent says no because you have school tomorrow. What matters to you, and what might matter to your parent?
Your parent asks you to stop playing a game right before you reach an important part. How might the timing feel to you, and what might your parent be thinking about?
You think your parent is angry because of their tone of voice. What else could explain how they sound?
Your parent seems distracted while you are telling them something. What are some possible explanations besides not caring?
Your sibling gets something you wanted and seems really excited. How might the same moment feel completely different to each of you?
Your sibling gets upset about something that seems small to you. Why might it feel bigger to them?
Your sibling does not want you in their room. What might privacy mean to them?
You want to borrow something from your sibling, but they say no even though they are not using it. How might they see the situation?
Your sibling copies something you do, and it annoys you. Why might they be doing it?
Your younger sibling gets more help from your parents than you do. What are some reasons they might need different help?
Your older sibling gets privileges that you do not have yet. What might your parent be considering?
You and your sibling both believe the other person started an argument. How could both of you remember it differently?
You accidentally bump someone in the hallway and they think you did it on purpose. What information does each person have?
Someone bumps into you and keeps walking without apologizing. What are some possible explanations?
Someone cuts in front of you in line. What could you find out before deciding they did it intentionally?
A classmate takes the seat you usually use. What are some possible reasons besides trying to bother you?
Someone uses your pencil without asking. What might they have assumed?
A friend forgets to return something they borrowed. What are some explanations besides not respecting your things?
Someone does not follow through on something they promised. What could have happened?
A friend forgets your birthday. What are some possible explanations, and how might you still feel about it?
You forget something important to your friend. How might the situation look from their perspective?
You arrive late and everyone else is annoyed because they had to wait. How might the situation feel different to you and to them?
Your team loses because someone makes a mistake at the end of the game. How might that person be feeling?
A teammate makes a mistake and another player starts yelling at them. How might each person be experiencing the moment?
You make a mistake that affects your whole group. What might your teammates be thinking, and what might they not know about what happened?
Someone celebrates loudly after beating you in a game. What might they be feeling even if their celebration annoys you?
You win a game easily against someone who is struggling. How might the game feel different to each of you?
A friend quits a game after losing several times. What might be happening for them?
Someone gets angry when they lose. What feelings might be underneath the anger?
You are excited because you won, but your friend is disappointed because they lost. How could you celebrate without ignoring how they feel?
A friend gets something you really wanted. What might you feel, and what might they feel at the same time?
You accomplish something and your friend does not seem excited for you. What are some possible reasons?
Someone brags about something they accomplished. What might they be hoping other people will notice?
A friend keeps comparing their work to yours. What might they be feeling?
Someone says, “That was easy,” after an assignment you found really difficult. Does that mean it should have been easy for you too?
You finish an activity quickly while another person needs much longer. What are some reasons people might need different amounts of time?
Someone learns a new skill much faster than you do. What does that tell you, and what does it not tell you?
A friend is really good at something but still gets nervous before doing it. Why might someone feel nervous even when they are skilled?
Someone refuses to perform in front of other people even though they practice all the time at home. What might make the situations feel different?
You invite someone to play and they say no. What are some possible reasons that are not about whether they like you?
You ask someone a question and they do not answer. What could be happening?
You say something and someone makes a confused face. What might they need from you?
Someone gives you an answer that seems rude. What could you check before deciding they meant to be rude?
A friend uses a different tone than usual when answering you. What are some things that could affect their tone?
You think someone is mad at you because they are quiet. What else could explain their behavior?
You think someone is bored because they are not looking at you while you talk. What else could be happening?
Someone does not make much eye contact while talking with you but keeps answering your questions. What are some ways they could still be paying attention?
A classmate moves around a lot while listening to the teacher. Does moving necessarily mean they are not listening?
Someone covers their ears in a noisy room. What might the room feel like to them?
Someone does not want to eat a food everyone else likes. What might their experience of that food be different from yours?
Someone becomes overwhelmed somewhere that feels perfectly comfortable to you. What does that tell you about how different people can experience the same place?
You love surprises, but your friend hates them. What might make surprises feel fun to one person and stressful to another?
You want a hug after a hard day, but your friend wants to be left alone when they are upset. How can both needs make sense?
You like talking when you are upset, but your sibling wants quiet. How could each person get what they need?
You think helping means fixing the problem, but your friend says they only want you to listen. What could you do?
You are trying to be funny, but someone thinks you are being mean. What matters more for figuring out what to do next: what you meant or how it affected them?
Someone hurts your feelings without meaning to. Can you believe it was an accident and still be hurt?
You accidentally hurt someone’s feelings. Can you have good intentions and still need to repair what happened?
You and another person disagree about what happened. What question could you ask to understand their side better?
Someone reacts in a way that makes no sense to you. What could you ask instead of guessing?
You are sure you know why someone did something. What is one other explanation you could consider?
You hear only one person’s side of an argument. What information might you still be missing?
Two friends tell you completely different versions of the same argument. What questions could help you understand what happened?
You watch two people disagree. What might each person want the other one to understand?
You disagree with someone’s choice but understand why they made it. How is understanding different from agreeing?
Someone disagrees with your choice but understands why you made it. What might respectful disagreement look like?
You learn new information that changes how a situation looks. What could you do if you realize your first assumption was wrong?
You find out someone had a reason for their behavior that you never considered. How might that change what you do next?
You cannot tell what someone is thinking or feeling. What could you ask instead of trying to read their mind?
You notice several clues about how someone might feel, but you are not sure. How could you check whether your guess is right?
You and another person experienced the exact same event but felt completely differently about it. How can both experiences be real?
You want someone to understand your side of a disagreement. What could you ask them after you explain it to see how they see the situation?
You are trying to understand someone else’s side, but you still disagree. What could you say that shows you understand without pretending you agree?

promptDecks.title: Thought Detective
promptDecks.description: Helps clients examine difficult thoughts more closely by separating facts from assumptions, weighing evidence, considering missing information, and questioning conclusions before accepting them as true.

prompts.text: Think of a thought that's been bothering you lately. What makes the thought feel believable?
Think of a thought you believe strongly when you're upset. What facts actually support it?
Think of a difficult thought you've had recently. What facts don't fit with the thought?
Think of a thought that feels completely true. What would you need to know before you could be certain?
Think of something you're worried will happen. What evidence suggests it might happen, and what evidence suggests it might not?
Think of something you're afraid is true about yourself. What evidence would a fair detective look for before reaching a conclusion?
Think of a negative conclusion you've made about yourself. What experiences don't fit that conclusion?
Think of something you believe you're “bad at.” What evidence shows a more complete picture?
Think of a time your brain told you that you couldn't handle something. What happened when you actually faced it?
Think of a thought that says you've “always” been a certain way. What examples can you find that don't fit “always”?
Think of a thought that says something “never” works out for you. What exceptions can you find?
Think of a thought that uses “everyone” or “no one.” Who doesn't completely fit that statement?
Think of something your brain treats as proof that you're not good enough. What else could that same information mean?
Think of a mistake your brain uses as evidence against you. What would be a fairer conclusion based on one mistake?
Think of a success your brain tends to dismiss. Why should that success count as evidence too?
Think of a compliment you've had trouble believing. What evidence might the other person have been noticing?
Think of a strength you sometimes forget you have. What real examples prove that strength exists?
Think of a situation where you assumed someone was judging you. What did you actually know, and what did you assume?
Think of a situation where you thought someone was angry with you. What evidence did you have?
Think of a situation where someone's behavior felt personal. What other information would you want before deciding it was about you?
Think of a time someone's facial expression or tone made you assume something. What are some other reasons they might have looked or sounded that way?
Think of a time someone didn't respond to you. What did you know for sure, and what did your brain fill in?
Think of a time someone's message seemed rude, annoyed, or unfriendly. What information was missing?
Think of a time you thought someone didn't like you. What evidence supported that conclusion? What evidence didn't fit it?
Think of a time you felt left out. What facts did you have about why it happened?
Think of a social situation you're uncertain about. What would you need to learn before you could confidently explain what happened?
Think of something you're worried another person thinks about you. How could you possibly know whether that thought is accurate?
Think of a situation where you assumed you knew someone's intention. What other intentions could explain the same behavior?
Think of a disagreement you've had. Which parts are observable facts, and which parts are interpretations?
Think of a situation where two people remember what happened differently. What evidence might help you understand the fuller picture?
Think of something you're predicting will go badly. What is the prediction based on?
Think of something you're nervous about trying. Have you faced anything similar before? What happened?
Think of something your brain says will be “a disaster.” What would actually have to happen for that word to be accurate?
Think of something your brain says you “won't be able to handle.” What difficult things have you handled before?
Think of an outcome you're afraid of. If it happened, what options or supports would you still have?
Think of something you feel certain will happen. What information could change your prediction?
Think of a prediction you've made before that turned out to be wrong. What did your brain miss?
Think of a time something went better than you predicted. What does that tell you about how accurate predictions can be?
Think of a time something did go badly. Did every part of your prediction come true, or was reality more complicated?
Think of a situation where uncertainty feels uncomfortable. Is your brain treating “I don't know” as if it means “something bad will happen”?
Think of a thought that begins with “What if...?” What would a detective need to investigate before deciding the “what if” is likely?
Think of a thought that begins with “I know they're going to...” What do you actually know?
Think of a thought that begins with “They probably think...” What evidence would you need to know what they actually think?
Think of a thought that begins with “This means...” What are some other things the situation could mean?
Think of a thought that begins with “It's because...” How many other possible causes can you identify?
Think of a thought that begins with “I can't...” Is the evidence saying “can't,” “haven't yet,” “don't know how,” or “this is really hard”?
Think of a thought that begins with “I'm terrible at...” What would a more complete review of your ability include?
Think of a thought that begins with “Nobody...” What people or experiences might be missing from that conclusion?
Think of a thought that begins with “I always...” What exceptions would a detective notice?
Think of a thought that begins with “I should...” Where did that rule come from, and what evidence says it has to be true?
Think of something you blame yourself for. What parts were actually within your control?
Think of something you feel completely responsible for. What other people, circumstances, or factors also affected the outcome?
Think of something you regret. What information did you have when you made the decision, rather than what you know now?
Think of a decision you're criticizing yourself for. What circumstances would a fair assessment need to consider?
Think of something that didn't work out. Does the outcome prove something about you, or only tell you what happened that time?
Think of a failure your brain has turned into a statement about who you are. What is the difference between “this went badly” and “I am bad”?
Think of a strong feeling you're having. What does the feeling tell you, and what does it not prove?
Think of a time you felt afraid even though you were safe. What does that tell you about the difference between feeling danger and being in danger?
Think of a time you felt rejected but later learned the situation wasn't about you. What did you originally assume?
Think of a time you felt certain about someone's intentions and later found out you were wrong. What information had been missing?
Think of a time you changed your opinion after learning something new. What new evidence mattered?
Think of a belief you've held about yourself for a long time. If you were investigating it for the first time today, what evidence would you examine?
Think of a belief about yourself that may have started because of something that happened years ago. Does current evidence still support the same conclusion?
Think of something another person once said about you that stuck. Does one person's statement deserve to count as a fact?
Think of a label you've given yourself. What information gets left out when you reduce yourself to that label?
Think of a harsh thought about yourself. Would you use the same evidence to reach that conclusion about someone else?
Imagine you're investigating the thought “Nobody likes me.” What evidence would you collect before deciding whether it's accurate?
Imagine you're investigating the thought “I'm going to embarrass myself.” What questions would you ask?
Imagine you're investigating the thought “I ruin everything.” What evidence would challenge the word “everything”?
Imagine you're investigating the thought “I can't handle this.” What evidence from the person's past would you look for?
Imagine you're investigating the thought “Everyone is judging me.” What would count as actual evidence rather than a guess?
Imagine you're investigating the thought “If I make a mistake, people will think I'm stupid.” What information would you need before accepting that conclusion?
Imagine you're investigating the thought “My friend didn't answer because they're mad at me.” What other evidence or explanations should you consider?
Imagine you're investigating the thought “I failed, so there's no point trying again.” What evidence is missing from that conclusion?
Imagine you're investigating the thought “Things are never going to get better.” What kind of evidence would be important to examine before treating that prediction as a fact?
Imagine you're investigating the thought “Nothing I do matters.” What small pieces of evidence might be easy to overlook when you're feeling discouraged?
If a thought were on trial, what evidence would the side arguing for it present?
If the same thought were on trial, what evidence would the side arguing against it present?
If you had to argue the opposite side of one of your strongest thoughts, what would you say?
If someone who knows you well investigated one of your negative beliefs about yourself, what evidence might they add?
If you could interview three people who know you in different parts of your life, what might each person notice that your current thought leaves out?
What question could you ask yourself when a thought feels true but you aren't sure whether it is?
What information are you most likely to overlook when you're upset?
What kinds of evidence does your brain tend to notice first when you're anxious, angry, or discouraged?
Does your brain give negative evidence more weight than positive evidence? What is an example?
What would it mean to evaluate a thought fairly rather than trying to prove it wrong?
How can you question a thought without forcing yourself to believe the opposite?
What is one thought you might be treating as a fact without enough evidence?
What is one belief you'd like to investigate more carefully instead of automatically believing?
What is one conclusion about yourself, another person, or the future that might deserve another look?
What is something you tend to believe about yourself when things go wrong?
What is something you tend to believe about yourself when you feel rejected?
What is something you tend to believe about yourself when you make a mistake?
What belief about yourself seems to show up in many different situations?
What belief about other people tends to affect how you respond to them?
What belief about the world influences how safe or confident you feel?
What do you tend to assume a difficult situation says about you?
When something goes wrong, what conclusion do you make about who you are?
What is a negative belief about yourself that feels true even when you know it may not be completely accurate?
What experiences may have helped you develop a difficult belief about yourself?
When do you remember first starting to believe something negative about yourself?
What messages have you received from other people about who you are?
What experiences have reinforced a belief you have about yourself?
What experiences do not fit a negative belief you have about yourself?
What evidence supports a difficult belief you have about yourself?
What evidence challenges a difficult belief you have about yourself?
What facts might a negative belief about yourself be leaving out?
What strengths are difficult to remember when a negative belief about yourself shows up?
What positive qualities about yourself do not fit the negative story your mind tells?
What would someone who knows you well say about a negative belief you have about yourself?
What would you say to a friend who believed the same negative thing about themselves?
What is one example of a time when a negative belief about yourself was not true?
What is one accomplishment that challenges a negative belief you have about yourself?
What is one relationship that challenges a negative belief you have about yourself?
What is one choice you have made that challenges a negative belief you have about yourself?
What is one strength that challenges a negative belief you have about yourself?
What is a belief about yourself that used to feel true but no longer does?
What belief about yourself has changed as you have gotten older?
What belief about yourself would you like to question more?
What belief about yourself might belong to an earlier version of your life?
What belief about yourself may have helped protect you in the past but causes problems now?
What happens when you treat a belief about yourself as a fact?
How does a negative belief about yourself affect the choices you make?
How does a negative belief about yourself affect your relationships?
How does a negative belief about yourself affect what you expect from other people?
How does a negative belief about yourself affect what you are willing to try?
What do you avoid because of something you believe about yourself?
What opportunities might you notice if you believed something different about yourself?
What would you do differently if you were less convinced by a negative belief about yourself?
What is a more balanced way to describe yourself?
What is a more complete version of a negative belief you have about yourself?
What could be true about you at the same time as the thing you criticize yourself for?
What belief about yourself would leave room for both your strengths and your struggles?
What would you rather learn to believe about yourself?
What experiences could help you test a new belief about yourself?
What small action could help you gather evidence for a healthier belief about yourself?
If your negative belief about yourself were a detective, what evidence might it be ignoring?
If your negative belief could only show evidence that supported its case, what would be missing?
If you put a negative belief about yourself on trial, what evidence would the defense present?
If your younger self developed a difficult belief for a reason, what might they have been trying to understand?
If your Wise Mind responded to a negative belief about yourself, what would it say?
If someone who cared about you described you fairly, what might they say that your negative belief leaves out?
If you woke up tomorrow no longer believing one negative thing about yourself, what would you do differently?
What is one old belief about yourself you are ready to investigate instead of automatically believing?
What is one piece of evidence you want to remember the next time a negative belief about yourself shows up?
What is one more balanced belief about yourself that you want to practice?
What is one sentence you want to remember when an old belief about yourself feels completely true?

promptDecks.title: Getting Through the Hard Days
promptDecks.description: Helps clients navigate periods when depression feels especially heavy by identifying what makes difficult days more manageable, reducing pressure, staying connected, and focusing on getting through the present moment rather than solving everything at once.

prompts.text: How do you know when you're having a particularly hard day?

promptDecks.title: Worst Case, Best Case, Most Likely
promptDecks.description: Helps clients move beyond catastrophic predictions by considering a range of possible outcomes, identifying what is realistically most likely, and recognizing how they could cope even if a difficult outcome occurred.

promptDecks.title: Cognitive Continuum
promptDecks.description: Helps clients move beyond all or nothing judgments by placing experiences, abilities, traits, and outcomes on a continuum, noticing the space between extremes, and developing more accurate and flexible ways of evaluating themselves and situations.

prompts.text: Think of something you're judging as either a success or a failure. What possibilities exist between those two?
Think of something you believe you either did perfectly or ruined. Where would the actual outcome fall between those extremes?
Think of something you consider a bad day. How bad was it from 0 to 100?
Think of something you consider a good day. Does a good day have to be 100% good?
Think of something that went badly. What parts went okay?
Think of something that went well. What parts were still difficult?
Think of a situation you describe as a disaster. Where would it fall between inconvenient and truly catastrophic?
Think of a problem that feels enormous. How serious is it from 0 to 100?
Think of something that feels impossible. Where would it fall between easy and impossible?
Think of something that feels unbearable. Where would it fall between comfortable and completely unbearable?

Think of something you don't feel ready for. How ready are you rather than simply ready or not ready?
Think of something you don't feel confident about. How confident are you from 0 to 100?
Think of something you're afraid to do. How much courage would it actually require?
Think of something you believe you can't do. Could “can't” actually mean difficult, unfamiliar, uncomfortable, or not yet?
Think of something you believe you're bad at. Where would your actual ability fall between no skill and complete mastery?
Think of something you're learning. Where are you between knowing nothing and knowing everything?
Think of something you haven't mastered yet. What can you already do?
Think of something you struggle with. Are you equally bad at every part of it?
Think of something you believe you're “terrible” at. What would someone who was truly at the very bottom of the scale look like?
Think of something you believe you're not good enough at. What would “good enough” actually look like?
Think of something you believe you need to be excellent at. What would competent look like instead?
Think of something you believe you need to get completely right. How right would it actually need to be for the outcome to be okay?
Think of a task you want to do perfectly. What would 90% look like?
Think of a task you want to do perfectly. What would 75% look like?
Think of a task you want to do perfectly. What would “good enough for this situation” look like?
Think of something where you believe anything less than your best isn't worth doing. Would 50% effort still accomplish something?
Think of something you haven't done because you can't do all of it. What would doing 10% accomplish?
Think of something you believe either counts or doesn't count. Could partial effort count?
Think of progress you've made. Where were you when you started, and where are you now?
Think of a goal you haven't reached yet. Does not reaching the endpoint mean you haven't moved?
Think of something that has improved but isn't completely better. How much has changed?
Think of a symptom or struggle that still happens. Is it happening as often, lasting as long, or affecting you as strongly as before?
Think of something you still find difficult. Are you recovering from it differently than you used to?
Think of something you thought you'd “fixed” that happened again. Does recurrence erase previous progress?
Think of a setback. How far back did it actually set you?
Think of a setback that makes you feel like you're back at the beginning. What skills or knowledge do you still have that you didn't have at the beginning?
Think of something you haven't done consistently. How often **have** you done it?
Think of a habit you're trying to build. What exists between doing it every day and never doing it?
Think of a goal where you missed one day. How much of the overall effort does that one day represent?
Think of a goal where you've had several difficult days. What percentage of the time have you still been moving toward it?
Think of something you describe as “I never do this.” When was the last exception?
Think of something you describe as “I always do this.” How often does it actually happen?

Think of something you describe as “everything is going wrong.” What isn't going wrong?
Think of something you describe as “nothing is working.” What is working even slightly?
Think of something you describe as “nothing has changed.” What has changed, even if it isn't enough yet?

promptDecks.title: Pie Chart Responsibility

promptDecks.title: Decatastrophizing
promptDecks.description: Helps clients examine feared outcomes without dismissing them, distinguish difficult situations from true catastrophes, and recognize the choices, coping abilities, supports, and next steps that would remain even if something went wrong.

promptDecks.title: Body Language
promptDecks.description: Helps clients recognize and interpret nonverbal communication, including facial expressions, posture, gestures, tone, and personal space, while exploring how their own body language can affect social interactions.

prompts.text: You are talking to someone who keeps looking at the clock. What might their body language be telling you?

promptDecks.title: Prediction vs. Reality
promptDecks.description: Helps clients compare what they expect or fear will happen with what actually occurs, identify patterns in their predictions, and build more accurate expectations through real world evidence and experience.

promptDecks.title: Thinking Traps
promptDecks.description: Helps clients recognize common thinking traps, understand how they can distort interpretations and intensify emotions, and practice noticing when their brain may be presenting an incomplete or exaggerated version of a situation.

Yes. For Puppet Play specifically, I would add more. Because you work with little kids, this isn't a deck I'd worry about making unusually large. Puppets are versatile enough that a big deck gives you genuinely different ways into play rather than just redundancy.

The current rebuild is strongest for roughly 6–10. I'd add a substantial group that works better for 3–6-year-olds: simpler language, concrete action, silliness, caregiving, family/home themes, separation/reunion, control, safety, sensory/body states, and very basic social problems. Little kids often communicate much more through what the puppet does than by answering “why” questions.

promptDecks.title: Reframe It
promptDecks.description: Description: Helps clients transform rigid, harsh, or unhelpful thoughts into more balanced and useful perspectives without relying on unrealistic positivity or pretending difficult situations are okay.

prompts.text: Think of a difficult thought you've had recently. What would be a more balanced way to say it without pretending everything is okay?
Think of a thought that makes a situation feel hopeless. How could you rewrite it to leave room for uncertainty or change?
Think of a thought that makes a problem feel impossible. What version acknowledges that it's hard without deciding you can't handle it?
Think of a thought that begins with “I can't.” How could you rewrite it to describe what is difficult rather than what is impossible?
Think of a thought that begins with “I'll never.” What would be more accurate based on what you actually know right now?
Think of a thought that begins with “This always happens.” How could you rewrite it without using “always”?
Think of a thought that begins with “Nothing ever works out.” What would a more complete version include?
Think of a thought that begins with “Everyone thinks...” How could you rewrite it without assuming you know what everyone thinks?
Think of a thought that begins with “They definitely...” How could you leave room for explanations you don't know yet?
Think of a thought that begins with “I know this is going to...” How could you turn the prediction back into a possibility rather than a certainty?
Think of a thought that begins with “What if something goes wrong?” What could you add that reminds you what you could do if it did?
Think of something you're nervous about. How could you change “This is going to go badly” into a thought that is realistic but makes trying possible?
Think of something uncertain. What could you tell yourself that acknowledges you don't know what will happen?
Think of something you can't control. What thought could redirect your attention toward what you can control?
Think of something difficult you need to do. What thought would help you focus on the next step instead of the entire challenge?
Think of a mistake you've made. How could you describe what happened without turning the mistake into a judgment about yourself?
Think of a mistake that triggered “I'm stupid,” “I'm a failure,” or another harsh label. What statement describes the actual mistake instead?
Think of something you regret. What could you tell yourself that takes responsibility without attacking who you are?
Think of something you wish you'd handled differently. What thought could help you learn from it instead of staying stuck in it?
Think of a time you didn't do as well as you hoped. What is a thought that makes room for both disappointment and another attempt?
Think of something you're still learning. How could you replace “I'm bad at this” with something more accurate?
Think of something that takes you longer than other people. What thought could acknowledge the difficulty without turning comparison into a judgment of your worth?
Think of something you haven't figured out yet. What difference does adding the word “yet” make?
Think of a setback. What thought would describe it as one part of the process rather than the ending?
Think of a time you needed help. What thought could make asking for help feel like a strategy rather than a failure?
Think of a time you felt embarrassed. What could you tell yourself that acknowledges the awkwardness without assuming everyone is judging you?
Think of a time you felt rejected. What thought could acknowledge the hurt without deciding it proves something negative about you?
Think of a time you felt left out. What could you tell yourself when you don't actually know why it happened?
Think of a time someone didn't answer your message. What is a balanced thought you could use until you have more information?
Think of a time someone seemed annoyed with you. What thought could keep you from assuming you know exactly what they're thinking?
Think of a time someone's behavior hurt your feelings. What thought could validate the hurt without automatically deciding what their intention was?
Think of a disagreement. How could you replace “They don't understand me at all” with something that leaves room for a more complicated reality?
Think of a time someone criticized you. What thought could help you decide whether any part of the feedback is useful without accepting every part as true?
Think of a time someone didn't like a choice you made. What thought could remind you that disagreement and rejection aren't necessarily the same thing?
Think of a time you compared yourself with someone else. What thought could make the comparison more complete or fair?
Think of someone who seems better than you at something. What thought could acknowledge their strength without turning it into evidence against you?
Think of a time someone else's success made you question yourself. What could you tell yourself that allows both things to be true: they are doing well, and your path still matters?

Think of something you don't like about yourself. Can you describe it without making it your entire identity?
Think of something you want to change about yourself. What thought could support change without requiring you to dislike yourself first?
Think of something you feel insecure about. What thought could acknowledge the insecurity without agreeing with everything it says?
Think of a time you felt like you weren't good enough. What would a more precise description of what you were struggling with sound like?
Think of a situation where you blame yourself for everything. How could you rewrite the thought to include the other factors that mattered?
